courses.title: Forensic Medicine and Toxicology
courses.description: Medico-legal practice in Nigeria, death and post-mortem changes, injuries, sexual offences, clinical toxicology and medical jurisprudence.

topics.title: Death and Post-mortem Changes
topics.summary: Diagnosis of death, early and late post-mortem changes, and estimating time since death.

material.heading: Death
material.body: Somatic (clinical) death is the irreversible cessation of circulation and respiration or of all brain function (brainstem death — deep coma of known cause, absent brainstem reflexes and apnoea test, after excluding reversible causes such as drugs, hypothermia and metabolic disturbance). Molecular (cellular) death follows over hours as individual cells die. The death certificate records the cause of death sequence: Part I — (a) the immediate cause, due to (b), due to (c) the underlying cause (the disease or injury that initiated the chain — the most important for statistics); Part II — other significant contributing conditions. Modes of death (e.g. 'cardiac arrest', 'respiratory failure') should not be used as causes. Deaths that are sudden, unexpected, violent, unnatural, in custody or of unknown cause must be reported to the coroner (southern states — Coroners Laws) or relevant authority.
keyPoints: Part I (a)→(c): underlying cause at bottom

material.heading: Post-mortem changes
material.body: Early changes: algor mortis (cooling — roughly 1–1.5 °C per hour initially, influenced by environment, clothing and body size; less reliable in hot Nigerian climates), livor mortis (hypostasis — purple discolouration in dependent areas beginning 30 minutes–2 hours, fixed after about 8–12 hours; cherry-pink in carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning), and rigor mortis (stiffening from ATP depletion — begins in small muscles such as the eyelids and jaw at 2–4 hours, complete by about 12 hours, passes off by 24–36 hours; accelerated by heat). Cadaveric spasm (instant rigidity, e.g. grasping a weapon) is distinct. Late changes: putrefaction (greenish discolouration of the right iliac fossa at about 24–48 hours in hot climates, bloating, marbling, skin slippage), adipocere (moist conditions) and mummification (dry heat). Entomology (fly larvae) helps estimate time since death in decomposed bodies.
keyPoints: Livor fixed ~8–12 h; cherry-pink in CO

topics.title: Injuries and Wounds
topics.summary: Classification of wounds, firearm injuries, head injury, burns and asphyxia.

material.heading: Mechanical injuries
material.body: Blunt force causes abrasions (superficial epidermal loss — may show pattern of the object and direction), bruises/contusions (bleeding under intact skin; colour change over days is an unreliable guide to age) and lacerations (tearing — irregular edges, tissue bridges, bruised margins; over bony prominences like the scalp). Sharp force causes incised wounds (longer than deep, clean edges, no tissue bridges) and stab wounds (deeper than long — the most dangerous, penetrating vital organs). Defence injuries on the palms, forearms and backs of hands suggest an assault victim. Firearm injuries: entry wounds (usually smaller, with abrasion collar; soot and powder tattooing at close range; contact wounds may be stellate over bone) versus exit wounds (larger, irregular, everted, no abrasion collar). Chop wounds (heavy instruments such as machetes) are common in Nigerian assaults and communal clashes.
keyPoints: Entry: abrasion collar, soot; exit: larger, everted

material.heading: Head injury, burns and asphyxia
material.body: Head injuries: extradural haematoma (middle meningeal artery; lucid interval; skull fracture), subdural haematoma (bridging veins; elderly, alcoholics, shaken infants), subarachnoid haemorrhage, and diffuse axonal injury. Burns: estimate extent (rule of nines, Lund–Browder chart in children) and depth; a body found in a fire — soot in the airways and raised carboxyhaemoglobin indicate the victim was alive when the fire started; pugilistic attitude and heat fractures are post-mortem artefacts. Asphyxia: hanging (ligature mark oblique, rising to a knot — usually suicidal), strangulation (ligature mark horizontal; manual strangulation — fingernail marks, fractured hyoid in adults; homicidal), smothering, choking, and drowning (froth at nose and mouth, diatoms in bone marrow support ante-mortem drowning). Petechial haemorrhages occur in the conjunctivae in many asphyxial deaths.
keyPoints: Soot in airways = alive in fire

topics.title: Sexual Offences and Child Abuse
topics.summary: Examination of survivors, evidence collection, legal provisions and child maltreatment.

material.heading: Sexual assault
material.body: Management of a survivor of sexual assault: ensure safety and consent, take a careful history, perform a thorough examination with a chaperone (documenting injuries with body maps and photographs), collect forensic evidence (swabs from involved sites, clothing, fingernail scrapings, blood and urine for toxicology) maintaining a chain of custody, and provide care — emergency contraception, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (within 72 hours), STI prophylaxis, hepatitis B vaccination, tetanus prophylaxis where needed, and psychosocial support with follow-up. The absence of genital injuries does not exclude rape. In Nigeria, the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015, the Criminal Code (south) and Penal Code (north) define rape and related offences; the Child Rights Act protects minors. Sexual Assault Referral Centres (SARCs, e.g. Mirabel Centre in Lagos) offer integrated services.

material.heading: Child abuse
material.body: Child maltreatment includes physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional abuse and neglect. Warning signs of physical abuse: injuries inconsistent with the history or developmental stage ('babies who don't cruise rarely bruise'), delay in seeking care, multiple injuries of different ages, patterned injuries (belt, cord loops, cigarette burns), immersion burns with sharp demarcation ('glove and stocking'), fractures in non-ambulant infants (metaphyseal corner fractures, posterior rib fractures), and abusive head trauma (shaken baby — subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages, encephalopathy). Other Nigerian contexts: child labour, trafficking, child marriage, 'almajiri' neglect, and accusations of witchcraft. Doctors have a duty to protect children: document carefully, admit for safety if needed, and involve social welfare and police in line with the Child Rights Act.
keyPoints: Duty to protect; involve social welfare

topics.title: Clinical and Forensic Toxicology
topics.summary: General management of poisoning, common Nigerian poisons, antidotes and snakebite.

material.heading: General management
material.body: Assess and stabilise airway, breathing and circulation first. Identify the poison from history, containers, and toxidromes: cholinergic (organophosphate — SLUDGE/DUMBELS: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis; bradycardia, miosis, bronchorrhoea), anticholinergic (hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, delirium — antihistamines, TCAs, datura), opioid (coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression), sympathomimetic (tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, dilated pupils — cocaine, amphetamines) and sedative-hypnotic. Decontamination: activated charcoal (50 g adults, within about 1 hour, if airway protected; not effective for alcohols, metals, lithium, corrosives), skin washing for organophosphates; induced vomiting is not recommended. Enhanced elimination: urinary alkalinisation (salicylates), haemodialysis (methanol, lithium, salicylates). Specific antidotes are listed below. Kerosene ingestion by children (common in Nigeria from storage in drink bottles) risks aspiration pneumonitis — do not induce vomiting.

material.heading: Antidotes and common poisons
material.body: Antidotes: organophosphates/carbamates (common agricultural and suicide poisons in Nigeria, e.g. 'Sniper' dichlorvos) — atropine titrated to dry chest secretions, plus pralidoxime; opioids — naloxone; benzodiazepines — flumazenil (caution with seizures); paracetamol — N-acetylcysteine; methanol/ethylene glycol — fomepizole or ethanol and dialysis (methanol outbreaks from adulterated local gin 'ogogoro'); cyanide (cassava-derived; industrial) — hydroxocobalamin; iron — desferrioxamine; warfarin — vitamin K; heparin — protamine; digoxin — digoxin-specific antibody fragments; beta-blockers — glucagon; lead — chelation (DMSA, EDTA — the Zamfara lead poisoning outbreak from artisanal gold mining, 2010). Snakebite (carpet viper Echis ocellatus in northern Nigeria — coagulopathy tested with the 20-minute whole blood clotting test; spitting cobra; puff adder): immobilise, no tourniquet or incision, transfer quickly, give polyvalent/specific antivenom for systemic envenoming.

questions.stem: Salivation, lacrimation, urination, bronchorrhoea and pinpoint pupils suggest poisoning with:
questions.explanation: A cholinergic toxidrome.

questions.stem: The end-point of atropine therapy in organophosphate poisoning is:
questions.explanation: Titrate until secretions clear.

questions.stem: Coma, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils suggest:
questions.explanation: Naloxone is the antidote.

questions.stem: Vomiting should NOT be induced in a child who drank kerosene because of:
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons are highly aspirated.

questions.stem: Methanol poisoning from adulterated local gin is treated with:
questions.explanation: They block conversion to toxic formic acid.

questions.stem: The antidote for iron poisoning is:
questions.explanation: It chelates iron.

questions.stem: The 2010 Zamfara State outbreak that killed many children was due to:
options: Lead poisoning from artisanal gold mining
questions.explanation: Lead-contaminated ore was processed at home.

questions.explanation: Non-clotting blood indicates envenoming.

topics.title: Medical Jurisprudence and Ethics in Practice
topics.summary: Consent, confidentiality, negligence, the MDCN code and doctors in court.

material.heading: Legal duties
material.body: Valid consent requires capacity, adequate information (nature, purpose, risks, alternatives) and voluntariness; it may be implied, verbal or written (for procedures). In emergencies where the patient cannot consent, doctors may act in the patient's best interests. Children under 18 generally need parental consent, though mature minors may consent in some circumstances. Jehovah's Witnesses may refuse blood transfusion (an adult's informed refusal must be respected; for children, court orders may be sought). Confidentiality may be breached with consent, when required by law (notifiable diseases, court orders), or to protect others from serious harm. Negligence requires a duty of care, breach of that duty (judged by the Bolam test — practice accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion), and harm caused by the breach (causation).

material.heading: Regulation and the courts
material.body: The Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN), under the Medical and Dental Practitioners Act (Cap M8 LFN 2004), registers doctors and dentists and publishes the Code of Medical Ethics in Nigeria; serious misconduct is tried by the Medical and Dental Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal (with appeal to the Court of Appeal), with sanctions from admonition to erasure from the register. Examples of infamous conduct: sexual relationships with patients, improper advertising, fee-splitting, issuing false certificates, abandonment of patients and practising under the influence of alcohol. Doctors may give evidence as witnesses of fact or as expert witnesses (providing opinion); medical reports should be objective and factual. Documents such as medical certificates, death certificates and police medical reports (e.g. police forms for injuries) must be accurate. The Police Act and the 'Compulsory Treatment and Care for Victims of Gunshot Act 2017' require hospitals to treat gunshot victims immediately without waiting for a police report.
keyPoints: MDCN and Code of Medical Ethics
Witness of fact vs expert witness
